items.title: Barry Kernfeld interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 16, 2020
items.q: I actually don’t love his playing as much as I used to. I love his ballad playing but his beboppy stuff is too many notes and not enough space for my taste.

ctx.x: Yeah, that’s a long time ago. That was my Ph.D. dissertation, that’s what got me into this writing about jazz in a scholarly way. And I was writing about the Miles Davis Sextet and trying to ask the question how did these people go about improvising and see if it

could be analyzed in some sort of useful way, which is all an introduction to say that I actually don’t love his playing as much as I used to. I love his ballad playing but his beboppy stuff is too many notes and not enough space for my taste.

Again, very timely that you said that because I just got a gift from a fellow jazz educator of Cannonball Adderley Transcribed Solos. And I was looking, you know, at page after page, there’s not too many rests in there. But I want to pursue the thing about improvising a little bit because there’s a quote from you, “The romantic notion that jazz is generated entirely spontaneously” and it makes me think of people who have asked me and I’ve heard them ask other people, “What is this thing they’re doing?
